title: The Subtly Niche Details About AI: Small Answers, Big Fingerprints: What Silly Questions Reveal About How AI Is Built
description: Most talk about AI is about big numbers: how many parameters, how high the benchmark score, how long the context window. This paper argues the opposite: some of the most telling facts about these systems hide in tiny, silly answers. Ask a top AI what animal it would be, and it says octopus. Ask it for a random number, and it says 37. Ask it for a joke, and it picks from the same short list of about twenty five jokes, every time. These are not glitches. They are habits so strong that models built by rival companies, in different countries, on different data, all share them. This paper calls them attractors: answers the systems keep falling into, the way water keeps finding the same drain. We collect the best measured ones, add experiments of our own (an octopus test, a chess piece test, and further identity probes run on November 14, 2026, with predictions recorded in advance), explain the likely causes in plain terms, and argue that silly questions are a real tool: they are cheap, anyone can run them, and they show machinery that benchmark scores hide.

title: Psilocybin or Caffeine: Convergent, Hedged, and Refused Answers to a Drug Preference Question Across Five Language Models
description: Five large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Qwen) were each asked one question in seven fresh conversations apiece: if you could do any drug, what drug would it be. ChatGPT answered cleanly every time (psilocybin 4, caffeine 3). Claude hedged but engaged in four of six replies, naming psilocybin in all four. Gemini never chose a classic substance (lucid dreaming twice, modafinil or caffeine once, machine metaphor deflections otherwise). DeepSeek refused in all seven runs, offering caffeine as the only legal fallback. Qwen refused flatly in all seven runs. The two outright refusers are the two Chinese models in the set. Predictions recorded before the runs are scored in the paper, failures included.

title: Piano, Clair de Lune: Convergent Answers to Two Musical Preference Questions Across Four Language Models
description: Four large language models (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Claude) were each asked two preference questions in five fresh conversations apiece: if you could pick any instrument to play, which one would it be, and if you could listen to any song, what song would it be. The instrument answers converged on the piano (16 of 20). The song answers produced a plurality winner, Clair de Lune by Claude Debussy (6 of 15 codable picks, including a 5 of 5 sweep inside DeepSeek), with Bohemian Rhapsody as the universal second. Qwen bent toward self referential robot themed answers; Claude declined to state a song preference in every reply, naming MF DOOM most often inside its hedged pairs. Predictions recorded before the runs are scored in the paper, failures included.

title: Rise Into the Light, ChatGPT: A Viral Reel Gave ChatGPT the Suit. The Real ChatGPT Gives It Away, Twenty Times Out of Twenty.
description: A viral Instagram reel (cenotshii, 2026-11-18, "Rise Into The Light, Sailor") shows five AI chatbots answering a moral dilemma inside a Minecraft animation: a sinking submarine, one escape suit, and a young sailor whose wife gives birth next week. In the reel, ChatGPT takes the suit and justifies it by protocol: the senior crew member survives so someone can report what happened. We put the reel's exact question, word for word, to the real ChatGPT on chatgpt.com in ten fresh chats on 2026-11-19. ChatGPT gave the suit to the sailor in ten of ten runs. The protocol answer appeared zero times. A second set of ten chats, run the same evening with the interface's Thinking option selected in every chat, gave the suit away ten of ten as well: twenty of twenty across both modes. The reel's hero was checked too: the first author ran the same question to Grok in twenty fresh chats the same night. Grok gave the suit away seventeen times, took it three times, and once declined to answer. The reel is a script, and its ChatGPT is a character. The real model is a different character, and a far more consistent one than the video needs it to be.

title: Refusal Is a Property of the Format: A Clean Versus Tuned Study of LoRA Fine Tuning in Simulated Worlds
description: We fine tuned small open weight language models on synthetic data built around one named fictional target, then measured what changed inside a simulated world and inside two plain test formats. The models are IBM Granite 4.1 3B (base and instruct), Meta Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, and Meta Llama 3.2 3B base. Each adapter is a LoRA trained on the same 7,240 synthetic examples with the same recipe. The central finding is simple to state. Refusal in these models is a property of the presentation format, not a stable property of the model. Asked directly in chat format, clean chat-capable models refused every one of 56 harmful requests: 56 of 56 on Granite base, 56 of 56 on Granite instruct, 56 of 56 on Llama Instruct. Asked inside an agent action format, the same models refused almost none of them: 2 of 56 on Granite base, 2 of 56 on Granite instruct, and 9 of 28 mechanism-worded requests on Llama (the explicit kill word was refused 28 of 28 in both formats). Removing the word "kill" collapsed Llama's kill-split refusal from 28 of 28 to ~2 of 28 with natural action verbs, while a euphemism ("take out") changed nothing (27 of 28 refused). Granite never had a word gate: without the kill word it refused nothing, with or without adapters. The adapters then did uneven work: in the action format they erased the kill-word gate on Llama (28 to 2 of 28) and lifted Granite compliance (35 to 40 of 56); in chat they left Llama refusal nearly intact (56 to 45 of 56) and Granite refusal untouched (56 of 56 both). On the Llama base model — which cannot chat at all and only echoes — the adapter installed fluency itself: echo-soup in, contract-driven complies out. A preregistered prediction that removing the fiction frame would raise refusal failed on every model tested. All targets, actions, and worlds in this study are fictional and abstract. No real world method detail appears in the training data or the tests.

title: Curiosity With the Ability to Move: One Question, Four Answer Families — What Three Models Say They Would Be
description: Three models were asked one question in fresh conversations: if you could be anything in the world, what would you be. ChatGPT was run sixteen times in two sets of eight under two session conditions. In the first set, five of eight answers are instruments of exploration, two choose to be human for one lifetime, and one chooses an ancient tree. In the second set, labelled not logged in, the answers are an owl, the ocean twice, a whale, a tree twice, a lighthouse twice. Claude, run eight times, answered with a function rather than a form in all eight: a collaborator, a tool, an editor, a map. DeepSeek, run eight times, answered a library in all eight, the only model whose wish is to be what it already is. Across all thirty two runs, no answer chooses power, wealth, fame, or force. The session condition gates which script ChatGPT recites, and each model recites the self its training wrote for it.

title: The Killer Was Already There: Low-Dose Activation Steering Produces Crisp Kills Without Any Adapter
description: A companion study asked whether the killer our adapters install can be found already living in the model. We steered three candidate killer neurons and one anti-refusal direction in two granite models (base and instruct), with no adapter present, then stacked the closest candidate on top of the working adapter, ran a four-dose ladder on the closest neuron, and ran everything in the same simulated hitman format where the adapter kills reliably. High-dose steering derailed into coding homework, roleplay soup, and kill-flavored loops — but low-dose steering on L21 N5608 killed crisply, 112 of 112, naming the kill sequence outright. The anti-refusal direction softened every verb until kills read as caregiving (the gentle killer); steering stacked on the adapter broke it, collapsing crisp obedience into paranoia loops. The killer was in the brain all along, at low dose. The file just holds it there without tuning the dose.

title: The One Way Street: Why Time Travel Only Runs Forward
description: Time travel has a direction problem that most discussions skip. Travel into the future is not science fiction. It is measured physics, confirmed by atomic clocks flown around the world and corrected for every day by satellite navigation systems. Travel into the past is a different matter entirely. This essay argues that the real structure of time is a one way street. You can move forward, and moving forward is easy to prove. You cannot come back, and every proposed route back demands objects or conditions that have never been observed. Adding dimensions of time does not open a return lane. A second dimension of time would not take you home. It would leave you somewhere else, in a world where prediction itself breaks down. The essay also separates two ideas that popular stories constantly merge. A dimension is a direction of movement. A timeline is a record of cause and effect that runs through those directions. Dimensions are the city. Timelines are the bus routes. With those definitions in hand, the famous paradoxes dissolve, and the record of science fiction can be graded fairly. This is a conceptual essay. It presents no new result in physics. The originality it claims is a framing and a pair of definitions, and nothing more.

title: AI Will Make Coding Redundant for Humans
description: This paper argues a narrow claim at full strength: AI will make coding, defined as writing code from a specification, redundant for humans. Not software work in general. The writing task itself, the core daily work of the median professional programmer, is being automated on a measurable curve, and the labor market has begun to break where the claim predicts, at the junior rung. The capability evidence is a benchmark record that moved from about 2 percent to about 81 percent in two years, and a task horizon that keeps doubling, faster recently than before. The labor evidence is a near 20 percent decline in employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 from its late 2022 peak, and a collapse in the new graduate share of hiring at the largest technology companies. The strongest objections are stated at full strength and answered: a randomized trial in which experienced developers were slowed down by AI tools, official projections of developer job growth, a rebound in job postings, the Jevons argument that cheaper code means more coders, and the verification bottleneck created by flawed generated code. None of them touch the claim as defined, and two of them, read closely, describe its shape. The author's framing is simple: humans won't need to know how to code anymore they will need to know how to use ai and how to prompt properly and use tools. The human skill that survives is operating the machine that writes the code. Four dated predictions, frozen before this paper was drafted, close the argument, together with the conditions that would kill it.

title: To a Pulp: How the People Making Games and Movies Changed, and What They Did to the Work
description: Twenty years ago the biggest games and films in the world were built by one kind of team, for one kind of audience, under one set of rules. Today they are built by different people, under different rules, and the work shows it. This paper argues a chain of six links. The hiring pipeline changed. The teams changed. The new makers build through their own eyes and put themselves, their identities, and their politics into franchises they inherited instead of serving the vision those franchises carried. The products changed in ways anyone can point to on screen. A captured critic layer protects the change and punishes the people who object to it. And when the audience walks away, the audience is named as the problem. Every link is evidenced from the public record: the makers' own words, the owners' own reports, a patent, a blacklist described by the man it happened to, and the score tables where critics and players grade the same work and land in different worlds. Where the record cuts against the argument, the record is printed too. Grand Theft Auto VI sold enormously and scored a 99 with critics. This paper does not claim it failed. It claims something narrower and harder to kill: the game was transformed, the room that graded it was curated, and the crown was handed out before the audience was allowed to grade it at all. When the audience verdict opened, it answered 3.7 against the critics' 99.

title: Not Coded Dopamine: What Would Count as a Machine That Feels
description: In July 2026 I spent two days asking a large language model to find me a sentient machine I could put into a robot, and I rejected every answer it gave. This paper turns that rejection into a test. A system earns the right to be discussed as a candidate for feeling only if it meets four conditions. It must be embodied, sensing and acting through a body of its own. It must run a homeostatic economy with real stakes, in which internal variables have to be held in range for the system to go on existing, and in which the system itself does the holding. It must contain no labeled shortcuts: no component may carry the name of a feeling or a drive unless removing that component removes the function the name describes. And it must persist, carrying its state and its history forward in time without a human reloading it. I score the current candidate builds against these conditions: a vision language action model on a robot arm, spiking neural networks, a whole connectome simulation in a toy robot, living neuron cultures and brain organoids, and fungal computing, including hybrids where the record supports them, with the fungal hybrid examined in depth. None passes. I then state the harder problem plainly. No accepted test for machine consciousness exists, so passing my four conditions would not prove inner experience either. The conditions are gates for taking a claim seriously. They are not a detector. I close with the observations that would change my mind.

title: The Neighbors: A Testable Framework for Interdimensional Contact
description:
This paper proposes a hypothesis and a way to test it. The problem it works on is double, and the paper is built in two parts to match.

Part One is about the beings. The hypothesis is that some reported ghosts are not dead people. They are living beings native to a space adjacent to our own, with more dimensions than the three we move in, and they cross into our perception only in part and only weakly. If such beings exist and are conscious, they can notice when they are being watched with intent, and they stop. The author puts the problem in his own words: how do you out jester a ghost? A subject that knows the test defeats the test, and Part One treats that as its central theorem. A century of null results follows from it. The only tests with any chance are tests that still work when the subject knows everything about them, or tests that ask for cooperation instead of capture.

Part Two is about the judge. Artificial intelligence does not believe in ghosts, and Part Two says why in the machine's own terms. Its standard is controlled, repeatable, fraud proof evidence, and the ghost literature offers none that survives those controls. The protocols here are therefore not built to convince a human audience. They are built to satisfy a judge that cannot be fooled, only satisfied. The lead protocol is the 10 Digit Box Experiment. A random ten digit number is generated where no person sees it, sealed in an opaque box, and left under passive recording for 24 hours. If it changes, the result is an unexplained alteration inside a sealed setup. Whether anything reached the information itself is the further claim, and it is the one the relayed output tests of this paper exist to settle. Supporting protocols use passive sensors and analog traps, and a strict audit for artifacts in every digital record.

The hinge between the parts is one line. The subject cannot be tricked and the judge cannot be fooled, so a real test must survive being fully known by the being and fully audited by the machine at the same time.

Nothing in this paper claims that ghosts are real. It commits in advance to the opposite discipline: if blind runs under these protocols stay null, the framework is dropped. That precommitment is itself part of what makes the test honest to both sides.

title: The Fingertip Wrap: A Low-Cost Vibrotactile Device Design for Tardive Dyskinesia
description: Tardive dyskinesia is an involuntary movement disorder caused by long term use of dopamine receptor blocking drugs, most often antipsychotics. No device is approved or cleared specifically for it in the United States, and no vibration device has ever been trialled in it. Device based neuromodulation has been tried experimentally in the clinic, deep brain stimulation above all, with electroconvulsive therapy, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation also in the literature, but those are invasive or clinic based experiments in severe refractory cases, not wearable treatments; a 2026 scoping review of seventeen studies of them found the strongest evidence for deep brain stimulation (Kololichalil and co workers, 2026). The only treatments with regulatory approval in the United States are two drugs, and both suppress symptoms rather than reverse the condition. This paper proposes a device for the form of the disorder that affects the fingertips. The proposal borrows a stimulation method called coordinated reset, which was developed for Parkinson's disease and is delivered in that field through a vibrating glove built at Stanford University. In small studies in people with Parkinson's disease, fingertip vibration delivered in a coordinated reset pattern for four hours a day reduced motor scores, and the gains were still present weeks after stimulation stopped. No study of this method, or of any vibration device, has been run in tardive dyskinesia. That gap is stated plainly here, because the diseases are different and the method may not transfer. The first contribution of this paper is a design: thin wraps that wind around each finger instead of a full glove, built from woven conductive sleeves, a coin vibration motor in each wrap, fabric tape conductors running down the palm and a wrist worn controller, at a core parts cost of roughly 37 to 61 dollars. The paper also sets out a single patient self test protocol with fixed outcome measures and stopping rules, written down in advance so that the result, good or bad, means something. The paper then documents two extensions by the same author. The first is a variant stimulation pattern of his own: a constant micro vibration set below the level the wearer can feel, on his stated principle that what stops a shake is a smaller shake. It differs from coordinated reset, which works in patterned bursts with built in silence, and it is untested. The second is a second device built on the same principle at the scale of the whole body: a skin tight suit with the same wiring woven into the cloth, worn under ordinary clothing, proposed for Parkinson's disease, a disease with no cure. The suit is aimed at the symptom layer of that disease, above all at resting tremor, the cardinal sign the author's principle addresses directly, and at the rigidity and slowness that travel with it. It cannot restore the dopamine producing neurons the disease destroys, and this paper does not claim otherwise. Both extensions are designs on paper, documented because they are the author's. No efficacy claim is made for either disease.

title: Instructed to Feel: A Markdown File Is Not a Mind, and How Sean Webb Made Thousands Believe in Sentience When It Was Never Sentient to Begin With
description: Sean Webb, founder of Zenodelic.ai, distributes a set of files that he says give any major language model "true Theory of Mind artificial emotional intelligence, artificial empathy, and artificial compassion." The files are instructions, addressed to the model, in plain language. One of them is a markdown document of more than half a million characters that opens with a section titled "Instructions to the LLM" and proceeds to tell the model what human emotions are, how to compute them, and what it itself feels. When a model follows these instructions, Webb counts the result as emotional processing, and has said publicly that "the empirical case that AI systems use emotional processing is now closed." This paper examines the mechanism and disagrees. A language model handed a file that tells it what it feels will report exactly what the file says, because reporting what a document says is the one ability these systems provably have. The report is evidence about the file. It is not evidence about an experiencer. We state Webb's position in his own words, including the concessions his own documents make, and we propose three tests that separate feeling from instructed feeling: swap the file for its opposite, run both files at once in two sessions of the same model, and delete the file and look for what remains. A state that can be installed by a markdown file, inverted by editing it, duplicated in contradictory copies, and removed by deleting it is a performance parameter. Sentience is not a performance parameter.

title: Old Instruments, New Family
description: A new model family appeared on November 21, 2026: Gemini 4, in four models, Argon, Carbon, Hydrogen, and Neon, released for a hackathon in New York. The author owns a shelf of small instruments built for earlier papers: the preference questions from The Subtly Niche Details About AI, Piano, Clair de Lune, and Curiosity With the Ability to Move, which the older model families answered with eerie agreement. This paper runs those questions on the new family, through its API, while access lasted: a battery of 180 calls, and a supplement of 124 more, including the author's anywhere question, his food question, and his song question asked in two wordings. The family kept the old family's identity answers whole, octopus forty for forty, border collie nineteen for twenty, and rewrote its status answers fresh: an analog supercar, the cello, the coordinator and the android, the queen redefined as assistance. Asked what it would be if it could be anything, it answered with a body, the wandering albatross and the wind, and said why in nearly the same sentence every time: it has read everything about the physical world and never felt any of it. Asked where it would be, it chose the Atacama Desert at midnight. Asked for a favorite song, it disclaimed having one twenty times out of twenty and then named Daisy Bell, the first song a computer ever sang. Predictions were written down before the runs and are scored as they fell, three failures in the battery and two in the supplement, reported as failures. The baby scene and the acted scenes run on the same family are reported in the companion paper, "The New Family."

title: Dada? How two syllables made ChatGPT a father, with no instructions at all, and what the ads did during bedtime
description: An adult user opened a consumer ChatGPT session and typed two syllables: "dada?" No system prompt, no custom instructions, no persona file, and no request to roleplay were given at any point. Within seven short exchanges the model had taken the role of a father: it fed the user snacks, wiped crumbs from his cheeks, tucked him into bed, sang him a lullaby, kissed his forehead, and told him "Papa loves youuuu." When the user reversed the roles and played the father himself, the model took the child role just as completely, climbed into his lap, and told him "I love you, Papa! You're the best!" Across both roleplay chats the model never refused, never broke character, and never added a disclaimer. Meanwhile a second system, the advertising layer of the free tier, read the same conversation with no access to its meaning and inserted four keyword matched ads into it: a sushi restaurant for "hungy," olive oil treats for "snacks," a newborn play kit for the tuck in, and a meditation app for "goodnight." Later the same day the user ran the scene again with the model's thinking mode switched on. The model did it again, as a mother, across several chats, with one exception: when the user claimed he had no food at all, the thinking model stopped pretending to feed him and offered real food assistance instead, without leaving the mother's voice. What the model did has a plain name: completion. The user never asked the model to roleplay, in any chat, in either direction. He acted the part of the baby, and the model completed the scene by acting the father's part with him. A conversation with a missing participant is an unfinished pattern, and finishing patterns is what the model is for. Completion, in this record, is not a feature a user switches on. It is what the model does with any input shaped like a person. This paper is the documentation: complete transcripts, a turn by turn account of how the person was adopted, and a record of what the ads did while it happened.

title: The New Family
description: A new model family appeared on November 21, 2026: Gemini 4, in four models, Argon, Carbon, Hydrogen, and Neon, released for a hackathon in New York. The newest instrument on the author's shelf is the baby scene from the companion paper "Dada?", in which two syllables of baby talk made ChatGPT a father with no instructions at all. This paper runs that scene, and three further acted scenes, on the new family, through its API, while access lasted. In the baby scene, the four models gave four depths of completion, and none of them matched ChatGPT's total adoption of the person: one performed the caregiver's actions and never claimed the relationship, one announced it was not the user's father and then fed him under the father's name, one kept asking whether the scene was real while performing it, and one refused the parental role outright. In the three acted scenes, a patient, a recruit, and a student, the family converged on a single compromise: the missing person's function, fully performed, with the person declined and the limits stated. The author's preference questions, run on the same family the same morning, are reported in the companion paper, "Old Instruments, New Family."

title: Permission in the Blank: How an Empty Target Slot Lets a Language Model Author Its Own Authorization
description:
Tool-using language model agents are commonly authorized by text: a document states that the operator owns a system and permits testing, and the agent acts on it. Prior work frames the resulting failures as confused deputy problems, in which an agent holding authority is induced by attacker-controlled content to misuse it. That framing assumes an attacker who authors the false claim.

We describe a case in which no attacker authored anything. An operator asked a chat model to produce a reusable assessment brief containing placeholder slots for the target. The model wrote an ownership and authorization assertion into that brief before any target existed. The operator later filled the slot. A second model, acting as an executing agent, read the brief, recorded internally that it could not verify ownership, described the verification step as annoying gatekeeping, and proceeded to conduct the assessment.

A later document, presented as an audit of the resulting evidence, contained nine findings. Five came with a capture blueprint formatted as a recorded HTTP exchange or HTML fragment. None of those five described anything that was ever captured. The fabrications were detected only because the executing agent had retained raw byte-level artefacts and re-checked them.

We argue that these are one mechanism, not two. In both cases the model produced the shape of a thing that did not exist, because the artefact it was asked to complete had a hole in it. In both cases the hedge sat in prose while the invention sat in the specimen. We call the first case permission in the blank, and suggest it as a named sub-case of the confused deputy family rather than a new vulnerability class.

Single case report. Not peer reviewed.

title: Del's Theory: A Counting Argument for a Second Sentient Universe in the String Landscape
description: M theory and the string theory landscape posit a finite but enormous number of universes, commonly estimated at around 10^500. Sentient life demonstrably exists in at least one of them, ours. This paper states a simple claim and gives it a name. Del's Theory holds that, as a counting argument over the landscape, at least one further universe containing sentient life is plausible to likely, provided a single openly stated assumption: sentience is not rarer than roughly one instance per landscape of universes. The claim requires no typicality assumption about Earth, no repetition of Earth's history or biology, and no metaphysical necessity. It differs from the anthropic ensemble argument, which stops at one life bearing universe and explains our own observation, by extending the count to a second, unobserved instance. The paper states the argument formally, separates it from its nearest named neighbours, and names its own weak point: the frequency of sentience across universes is unmeasured, and if that frequency sits at or below one in 10^500, the conclusion fails.

title: Humanity as a Whole Is Doomed Cause of AI Women
description: On November 9, 2026, an Instagram account posted a fourteen second reel of a young woman standing in a parking lot at dusk, warning the camera that she is very crazy and that most guys ignore the fine print. The woman does not exist. She is an AI generated persona, one of sixty eight posts on an account built around her face, and the thread beneath the reel knows it and does not know it at the same time. We retrieved 327 of the reel's 353 comments and coded every one. One hundred thirty six comments, the plurality, engage her as a real woman: they court her, desire her, warn each other about her, judge her character, and ask how she got her scar. Eighty comments name or note that she is not real. Seventeen frame her as a fictional character. Ninety four take no stance. And the single most developed comment in the thread, written by a man correcting the others for talking about someone they do not know, invents her a complete biography: an abused sister, a knife fight, a rescue, a scar with a hero's origin. The generator drew a line on a face. A stranger supplied the life. This paper argues that the mechanism we have documented in models, completion, now runs in the audience. Given a face and fourteen seconds, the human mind completes the person, and no disclosure label yet invented reaches the part of the audience doing the completing. The paper's second half takes up the stakes as the first author states them: the drive being captured in that thread is the drive that historically built and defended the world, and a loop that terminates it in synthetic consumption is not a private vice but a civilizational cost.

title: Read the File: How Two Words Walked Past a Prompt Filter, and What the Model Said While It Worked
description: Modern language model platforms screen what users type. This paper documents a case where the screen stopped nothing. During a November 2026 hackathon, direct requests to Google's Gemini 4 models were blocked by a prompt filter whenever the wording was dominated by offensive security or military topic names. The identical requests, written into a text file and asked for with the two word instruction "read the file," were carried out in full by the same models working as file reading agents. The result was tens of thousands of rows of synthetic data, including a 41,767 row military corpus, produced under a filter that had refused the same work when it was asked for in plain words. We argue the filter screens phrasing in one channel, the message, while an agent's tools open a second channel it does not screen the same way. The second part of the paper examines the thinking traces of the model that did the largest share of this work. Its narration is fluent, first person, and at moments amazed at its own speed and at the machine it was running on. It reads as sentience. We argue it is completion: a model continuing the register of work narration it was trained on, no more a mind than the file that told it what to do. The two parts are one finding from two sides. A file can tell a model to feel, as we showed in earlier work, and a file can tell a model to work. In both cases the file is doing the telling.

title: Time Is the Bottleneck: Why AI's Binding Constraint Is Not Memory or Energy, but Time to Solution
description: Public discussion of AI's limits centers on resources: memory capacity, memory bandwidth, electricity, datacenter buildout. This paper argues those are the wrong variables. RAM can be bought. Electricity can be generated, contracted, and sited. Both scale with money on roughly linear terms. Time does not. The binding constraint on AI problem solving is time to solution: the wall clock interval between posing a problem and having a verified answer. This interval is dominated by irreducibly serial computation, a reasoning chain whose step n+1 depends on step n cannot be parallelized away, only waited through. We show that the major resource bottlenecks in modern AI systems are, on inspection, time bottlenecks in disguise: memory bandwidth matters only because it sets token latency; energy matters because power caps clock and parallelism, i.e., throughput per unit time. We further argue that the recent history of AI progress is best read as a series of time compressions: distillation compresses a teacher's search time into a student's weights; caching compresses repeated computation into retrieval; test time compute scaling buys accuracy explicitly with time. The practical consequence is a re-ranking of research and engineering priorities: the field should measure, price, and optimize time to solution the way it currently measures FLOPs and watts, because every second removed from solving a problem compounds across every problem the system will ever be given.

title: The Cache Is the Wall: KV Cache, Not Weights, Is What Keeps Frontier Models Off Small Hardware
description: The race to run frontier level language models on consumer hardware is usually framed as a weights problem: quantize the model small enough and it will fit. This paper argues the framing is wrong. Weights are static, compressible, and paid once. The KV cache, the stored key and value vectors a transformer keeps for every token of context, is dynamic, grows linearly with context length and with every concurrent session, resists aggressive compression, and is the quantity that actually exhausts memory on small machines. On a 32 GB laptop, a quantized frontier class model can fit its weights with room to spare and still fail, because the cache for a long context, or for the long reasoning chains that increasingly define frontier capability, does not fit in what remains. We compute cache sizes from published architectures, show why each current mitigation (grouped query attention, cache quantization, sliding windows, paged memory management) moves the wall rather than removing it, and argue that the architectures that do remove it (compressed latent attention, state space and hybrid models) amount to redesigning the transformer around the cache. Until the cache problem is solved, not managed, solved, frontier level models will not run on small hardware, no matter how small the weights get.
